newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD says coalition tax sums don't add up.
newsitem.headline: German SPD says coalition tax sums don't add up.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Friday government tax reforms would rip a huge hole in state finances and do nothing to reduce record post-war unemployment.

SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told parliament that the tax reforms would force up the total budget deficit to between 150 and 160 billion marks in 1999, a level which he said was "completely irresponsible".
Finance Minister Theo Waigel wants to cut the total public deficit to 105 billion marks this year -- or 2.9 percent of GDP -- sufficient to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).

Scharping said the SPD would only rejoin cross-party talks on tax reforms if the coalition met three conditions -- slash labour overheads in July, cut taxes for ordinary workers next year and put together solid counter-financing.
Scharping was speaking in a debate on the introduction of Waigel's 1998 tax bill, which would introduce the first stage of a two-year package of 30 billion marks in tax cuts.
The SPD, which broke off talks on reaching a tax consensus in a recent row over coal subsidies, can block most tax legislation with its majority in the upper house of parliament.
